unit.title: Weld using submerged arc welding process

summary: This unit teaches submerged arc welding (SAW): a mechanised process in which the arc burns under a blanket of granular flux, used for long, heavy seams on tanks, vessels, beams and pipe. You will learn how the process and its equipment work, how to choose and control wire and flux, prepare and set up joints, set and adjust the welding parameters, prevent and find defects, and plan, cost, lead and record SAW work to a welding procedure specification (WPS).

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It covers **submerged arc welding (SAW)**, the process used to make the long, heavy, high-quality seams on water and fuel tanks, pressure vessels, pipe, plate girders and ship and barge plate.

In SAW a bare wire is fed into the joint and the arc burns hidden under a layer of granular **flux**. The welding head is carried along the seam by a tractor or a boom, or the work is turned under it. The welder becomes an **operator**: the skill is in the set-up, the settings, the tracking and the checking, not in a steady hand.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and fabricators moving into tank, vessel and structural production work. Not every centre or shop in Jamaica has a SAW machine. Where yours does not, you will practise the set-up on a travel carriage, learn the theory from this kit, and may visit a shop that uses SAW.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the shop
rows: Explain the process and choose it
Say how SAW works, what it does well, its limits, and which jobs suit it better than MMAW, GMAW or FCAW.
Control high current, arc flash-through, flux dust, hot slag, moving rolls and carriages, and heavy wire coils and flux bags.
Name and check the power source, wire feeder, head, hopper, flux recovery, tractor, column and boom, turning rolls and earth.
Choose and control wire and flux
Read the wire-flux classification, choose fused or bonded, active or neutral flux, and store, dry, recover and record it.
Prepare joints to the WPS, fit backing and run-on and run-off tabs, align the tracking, set stick-out and flux depth, and dry-run.
Set current, voltage, travel speed, stick-out and polarity, and know what each does to the bead; work out heat input; weld circumferential seams.
Name SAW defects and their causes and cures, and choose the inspection and tests.
Work out arc time, weld metal, wire and flux, plan the job, brief the team and keep seam records.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on the process, safety, equipment, flux, wire and flux classification, parameters, joint preparation, circumferential seams, defects, procedures, inspection, calculations and leading the team.

A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as flux, hopper, tractor, stick-out, run-off tab, tandem, fines) and longer answers that explain the process, a set-up, the effect of the parameters, flux control or a job plan.

**Practical tasks**: setting up (and, where there is a machine, running) a SAW butt seam with run-on and run-off tabs, or the full set-up on a travel carriage; and writing a SAW procedure, job plan and flux control sheet for a water tank.

blocks.note: Many questions are about cause and effect: what happens to the bead when the current, voltage, speed or stick-out changes. Learn the table in the parameters section until you can say it without looking.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: How SAW works and when to use it

flow: A motor feeds bare wire from a coil through a copper **contact tip**, which passes the welding current into it
Granular flux flows from a **hopper** through a tube and covers the joint just ahead of the wire
The arc burns between the wire and the work, **hidden under the flux**
The heat melts the wire, the joint edges and some of the flux; the melted flux forms **slag** that protects and shapes the weld as it cools
The head moves along the seam (or the work turns under it) at a set **travel speed**
Unmelted flux is **recovered** for reuse; the slag is removed when the weld has cooled

blocks.p: Because the arc is covered, there is almost no arc light, little spatter and little visible fume. Because the process is mechanised, the current can be very high (often several hundred to over 1 000 amps), so SAW lays down far more weld metal, with deeper penetration, than manual processes.

head: Point
MMAW
GMAW / FCAW
SAW
rows: Typical deposit (kg of weld metal per hour of arc)
About 5–12 with one wire; much more with two
All (with the right mode or wire)
Flat, and horizontal fillets; horizontal butts only with special supports
Welder can adjust as he goes
Little: the machine cannot change to suit a varying gap
Costly and heavy; set up for each job
Long straight or round seams in thick plate, in the shop

ul: Long and circumferential seams on water, fuel and process tanks and pressure vessels.
Web-to-flange fillets on plate girders and built-up beams.
Longitudinal and spiral seams in large pipe, and plate butt joints for ship and barge decks.
Hardfacing and cladding (with strip or wire) on rollers and wear parts.
It does **not** suit short or awkward welds, vertical and overhead joints, thin sheet, or site work in every position.

head: Set-up
What it is
rows: One wire and one power source: the most common
Two thin wires side by side through one contact tip, on one power source, for more deposit
Two (or more) wires one behind the other in the same pool, each on its own power source. The lead wire (often DC+) gives penetration; the trailing wire (often AC) adds fill and smooths the bead
A wide strip electrode instead of wire, for laying corrosion- or wear-resistant layers

blocks.p: The hidden arc makes SAW look safe. It is not: the currents are very high, the slag and plate are extremely hot, and the work moves.

head: Hazard
Where it comes from
Controls
rows: Electric shock and burns from connections
Very high welding currents; cables, clamps and contact tips
Check cables and connections are sound and tight before the run
Isolate the set before changing tips, wire or rolls
The arc breaks through where the flux runs thin, at starts, or when flux is pushed aside
Suitable eye protection for the operator and anyone near the head
Keep the flux topped up and the arc covered
Never brush the flux aside to look at the arc
Filling hoppers, sieving and recycling flux, sweeping
Dust mask or respirator as the safety data sheet (SDS) says
Clean up by vacuum, not by blowing or dry sweeping
Slag often peels off in long, very hot strips; plate stays hot for a long time
Gloves, long sleeves and safety boots
Slag into a metal bin, away from anything that burns
Less than other processes, but some fume and fluoride gases are given off
Ventilation or extraction at the head
Trapping, crushing and entanglement at turning rolls and carriage wheels
Know and test the stop buttons
**Never reach across or under a turning shell** or into the rolls; stop them first
Wire coils (often 25 kg or more) and flux bags (often 25 kg)
Lifting aids or two people, as the rules say

blocks.note: A shell turning on rolls looks slow, but it does not stop for a sleeve or a hand. If flux spills onto a roll or the seam needs clearing, the rolls are stopped first. Only then does anyone reach in.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Brief the team on the stop buttons, the flash-through risk, flux dust and the hot slag before the first run.
Give each person one clear job during a run: operator, hopper and flux, tracking and meters, recorder.
Read the SDS for the flux and make sure the right mask is worn when hoppers are filled or flux is sieved.
Keep walkways round the rolls and the boom clear of cables, bags and offcuts.
Report and record injuries, near misses and damaged equipment.

head: Part
Its job
Check before use
rows: Gives a high current, usually DC, at a high duty cycle (many are rated 100% at 600–1 000 A). Most are constant-voltage with a constant wire speed; some large-wire sets are constant-current
Cables, connections and meters working; duty cycle suits the job
Pulls wire from the coil and pushes it through the head at a steady speed
Rolls the right size, pressure right, wire straightener set
Passes the current into the wire
Right size for the wire; not worn oval or burnt
Holds flux and lays it on the joint ahead of the wire
Right flux, dry, no lumps; flow even
Picks up unmelted flux by vacuum and returns it, often through a sieve and magnet
Filters and sieve clean; hose clear
A self-driven carriage that carries the head along a track or along the plate
Track straight and parallel to the seam; speed checked
Holds and moves the head over large work, such as a tank shell
Powered rollers that turn a cylinder under a fixed head
Spacing right for the diameter; shell turns evenly with no creep
Tilts and turns smaller work so the weld stays flat
Keeps the wire on the joint line (a guide wheel or finger, a laser, or the arc itself)
Set and checked on a dry run
Carries the current back; on turning work, a **rotating earth** keeps contact as the work turns
Tight, on clean metal, close to the seam
Set and show current, voltage and travel speed
Readings checked against the WPS during the run

head: Current
Effect
Used for
rows: Deepest penetration, best bead shape, steady arc
Most single-wire joining work on carbon steel
Wire melts faster (often about a third more deposit) with **less penetration**
Build-up, surfacing and cladding; sometimes thin plate
Penetration between the two; much less arc blow
Very high currents, and the trailing wire of a tandem set

blocks.p: At high DC currents, magnetic fields round the work can push the arc off line: **arc blow**. It is worst near the ends of seams and near heavy masses of steel. It is reduced by moving the work connection (or connecting at both ends), using run-on and run-off tabs, lowering the current, or using AC.

SAW wire is bare, solid steel wire, usually copper-coated to stop rust and improve contact, on coils or in drums. Common sizes are 2.4, 3.2, 4.0 and 5.0 mm. Keep it dry and clean: rusty or oily wire causes porosity and poor feeding.

head: Wire class (examples)
Manganese level
Typical use
rows: With active fluxes that add manganese
General carbon steel work; the most common
With neutral fluxes, or where higher strength is needed

blocks.p: A carbon steel SAW consumable is classified as a **wire and flux together**, because the weld metal depends on both. Example: **F7A2-EM12K**.

head: Part
Meaning in F7A2-EM12K
rows: Weld metal tensile strength at least 70 000 psi (about 480 MPa)
Tested **as-welded**. A **P** here would mean tested after post-weld heat treatment
Impact toughness tested at **−20 °F (about −29 °C)**: the weld metal must absorb at least about 27 J there. (0 = −18 °C, 4 = −40 °C, Z = no impact test)

blocks.note: Because the wire and flux are classified together, a WPS names the combination. A different flux, even of the same class from another maker, must be checked against the WPS; if the WPS does not cover it, the procedure must be requalified.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Type
How it is made
Points to know
rows: Ingredients melted together, cooled to a glass and crushed
Hard to add alloys or deoxidisers
Fine powders bonded into grains and baked
**Picks up moisture easily**: keep dry, often in a heated hopper
Grains break down into fines when handled roughly

head: Flux behaviour
What it means for you
rows: Adds manganese and silicon to the weld. More voltage melts more flux and adds more. Fine for one or two passes; on multi-pass welds, high voltage makes them **build up**, so the weld gets harder and more crack-prone. Keep to the WPS voltage and the maker's limits.
Changes the weld chemistry very little, whatever the voltage. Preferred for thick, multi-pass joints.
Adds alloying elements on purpose, for example for hardfacing or alloy steels.
Acid fluxes give smooth beads at high speed but lower toughness. **Basic** fluxes give **tougher** weld metal (for low-temperature or critical work) but are more sensitive to moisture.

flow: Store sealed bags off the floor in a dry store; rotate stock so the oldest is used first
Keep opened bonded flux in a heated hopper or flux oven if the WPS or maker says so
Re-dry damp flux at the maker's temperature and time (often about 250–350 °C for one to two hours for bonded fluxes), or scrap it
After welding, recover unmelted flux by vacuum or by sweeping clean flux, never slag and dirt
Sieve out slag lumps and pass it over a **magnet** to take out scale and bits of metal
Remove the **fines** (dust), and mix in new flux regularly as the maker advises
Record the flux type and batch number on the seam record

blocks.p: Moisture in flux gives off hydrogen in the arc: **porosity**, and **hydrogen cracking** in thick or high-strength steel. Too many fines pack the flux layer so gas cannot escape: the bead comes out rough and pock-marked.

blocks.note: Jamaica's humid air, especially in the rainy seasons and at yards near the sea, gets into an open bag of bonded flux within days. Close bags at once, keep the flux store dry, and do not leave flux in a cold hopper overnight.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: SAW penetrates deeply, so its joint preparations have **smaller groove angles and bigger root faces** than MMAW. A thin root face that suits a manual root run would simply be burned through.

head: Preparation
Typical use (always follow the WPS)
rows: Square edges, one run from each side (two-run technique)
Plate up to roughly 10–16 mm, depending on the current. The second run must penetrate past the middle and fuse into the first.
One-sided welds where the back cannot be reached
Double-V with a large root face (often about 5–8 mm)
Thick plate, welded from both sides; runs balanced between the sides; back gouging where the WPS asks
Web-to-flange and stiffener welds, in the horizontal (2F) position, or flat (1F) with the joint tilted to 45°

head: Backing
How it works
Watch for
rows: A grooved copper bar clamped tight under the joint holds up the pool and shapes the root; copper does not fuse to steel
It must be **tight** to the plate all along: where it drops away, the pool falls through
The arc must never melt it: copper in the weld causes cracking
A trough of flux pressed up under the joint (often by an inflated hose)
Ceramic tiles taped under the joint, removed after welding
A strip of the same steel, fused into the root and left in place
Allowed only where the drawing says
A root run made by MMAW, GMAW or FCAW, then filled with SAW
Sound, clean, and to its own WPS

ul: SAW cannot adjust itself to a gap that varies, so the fit-up must be accurate and even all along the seam: gap, root face, angle and alignment within the WPS limits.
The joint faces must be clean and dry: rust, mill scale, oil, paint, primer and water all cause porosity.
Tack welds must be **small, sound and fully fused**, made by a qualified welder with a low-hydrogen process, so the SAW run can melt them in completely. Cracked or porous tacks are ground out.

blocks.p: A SAW arc takes a short distance to settle, and the end of the run leaves a **crater**. So the run starts on a **run-on tab** and finishes on a **run-off tab**, fitted at the ends of the seam. The tabs are the **same steel and thickness** as the job, with the **same preparation**, so the arc behaves as it will on the job, and long enough (often about 50–100 mm) for the start and crater faults to stay on them. They are cut off afterwards.

blocks.h: Setting up a long butt seam

flow: Read the WPS: wire and flux, polarity, current, voltage, travel speed, stick-out, flux depth and pass plan
Check the preparation, fit-up and tacks; check the joint is clean and dry
Fit run-on and run-off tabs; fit the backing if used
Lay the track parallel to the seam, or set the guide or seam tracker
**Dry run** with the arc off along the whole seam: the wire tip must stay on the joint line all the way
Check the wire class and size, drive rolls, contact tip and the flux type and dryness
Fix the work connection close to the seam, on clean metal
Set the wire angle and **stick-out** (the length of wire from the tip to the arc, often about 25–35 mm)
Set the flux depth so the arc will be fully covered
Set the parameters and check them on a test run on scrap plate
Start on the run-on tab; watch the meters, flux cover and tracking; finish on the run-off tab

blocks.note: Do not try to look at the arc by brushing the flux aside. Read the meters, watch the tracking and the bead as it appears behind the flux, and keep the arc covered.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: The operator controls the weld through a few settings. Change **one at a time**, and stay within the WPS.

head: Setting
Raising it (with the others the same)
Too much
Too little
rows: Deeper penetration and faster melting: the **main control of penetration**
Burn-through; deep, narrow bead that cracks along its centre
Poor penetration and fusion; tall, narrow bead
**Wider, flatter** bead; more flux melted (more alloy pick-up with active flux)
Undercut; uneven bead; more flux used
Tall, narrow, peaked bead; slag hard to remove
Large bead; pool runs ahead of the arc; poor fusion; burn-through
Tip overheats; spatter under the flux
A **thicker** wire spreads the current: wider bead, less penetration, better at bridging a poorer fit-up. A **thinner** wire concentrates it: deeper penetration and faster melting
Too thick: shallow penetration, lack of root fusion
Too thin: deep, narrow bead; burn-through on a wide gap
Gas cannot escape: rough, pock-marked bead

blocks.note: Typical single-wire figures (always follow the WPS): 3.2 mm wire about 300–600 A, 4.0 mm about 400–800 A; arc voltage about 28–38 V; travel speed about 300–1 000 mm/min; stick-out about 25–35 mm.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **Heat input** is the energy put into each millimetre of weld. Too much makes the weld and heat-affected zone coarse and less tough; too little can leave hard zones that crack. Many WPSs give a maximum and a minimum.

ul: Slowing down raises the heat input; speeding up lowers it. Raising the current or voltage raises it.
Before changing speed or settings, work out the new heat input and check it is inside the WPS limits.
For SAW the full figure is used; some codes multiply other processes by an efficiency factor.

blocks.p: As a run freezes, it solidifies from both sides towards the middle. If the run is **deeper than it is wide**, the last metal to freeze, with the impurities, is trapped in a thin line down the centre, and shrinkage tears it open: **centreline (solidification) cracking**. Keep each run **wider than it is deep**: lower the current, raise the voltage a little, or open up the groove, as the WPS allows. Very concave fillet beads are also crack-prone.

ul: Set the rolls to the right spacing for the diameter and check the shell turns evenly without **creeping** along the rolls. Creep moves the seam out from under the wire; cure it by aligning the rolls or with anti-creep rolls before welding.

The **travel speed is the surface speed of the shell**. Time for one turn = circumference ÷ travel speed. Example: a 2 m shell has a circumference of π × 2 000 = 6 283 mm; at 600 mm/min one turn takes about 10.5 minutes. Check it by timing a marked length of shell with a stopwatch: speed = distance ÷ time, so a 1.2 m mark that passes the head in 2 minutes gives 1 200 ÷ 2 = 600 mm/min.
Use a **rotating earth**: a fixed clamp would wind its cable round the turning shell or tear off, and current passing through the roll bearings damages them.

On an outside seam, set the wire a short distance before top dead centre, on the side the surface comes up from, as the WPS or maker's table says (often about 15–50 mm, more on bigger shells). The pool then freezes as it passes over the top and does not run off. Too little offset gives a tall, narrow, deep bead; too much gives a flat, shallow bead, and slag may run in front of the arc.
On an inside seam the head works near the bottom of the shell and the offset is set the other way, again as the WPS says.
Dry-run a full turn with the arc off to check the tracking all the way round.
Where the run comes back to its start, overlap the start a short way and finish so there is no crater or unfused start.

Horizontal fillets (2F): the wire is angled into the joint and aimed slightly onto the bottom plate, as the WPS says. Aimed too high, or with voltage or speed too high, it undercuts the upright plate.
Single-pass horizontal fillets are limited in size; larger fillets are made in several runs, or flat (1F) by tilting the joint to 45°, which gives equal legs and deep, even penetration.

head: Defect
Main causes
Cures (within the WPS)
rows: Bead deeper than wide (high current, narrow groove)
Make runs wider than deep: lower current, a little more voltage, wider groove
Rust, oil, paint, primer or water on the joint
Flux too shallow (flash-through) or too deep, or too many fines
Correct flux depth; sieve out fines
Slag left between passes, often in a notch at the side wall
Wire badly placed so runs do not wet the side walls
Clean every pass fully; grind notches
Place runs to wet the side walls
Travel speed or voltage too high
Current too high or speed too slow
The arc has melted the copper backing bar
Correct settings; backing groove and position right
Bead too convex or too narrow; voltage too low; very hot plate
Flatter bead; correct settings; let the plate cool to the interpass limit

head: Method
Use in SAW work
rows: Every seam: profile, undercut, cracks, porosity, start and end of seam, tabs removed and ground
Surface cracks, especially on fillets, tab removal areas and back-gouged grooves
Inside the full weld on butt seams of tanks and pressure vessels: porosity, slag, lack of fusion, cracks
A cross-section cut, polished and etched shows the penetration, fusion, shape of each run and the heat-affected zone: used on trial and procedure plates
Procedure qualification: ductility, strength and toughness

flow: Write a draft procedure: plate, joint, wire-flux combination, polarity, current, voltage, travel speed, stick-out, passes, preheat and interpass
Weld a test plate while an inspector records the actual values
Inspect it visually and by RT or UT
Cut test pieces for bend, tensile and, where needed, impact tests and a macro
If they pass, record the results on the **procedure qualification record (PQR)** and issue the WPS with ranges based on it

blocks.p: Changes that usually need a new or requalified procedure include: a different wire-flux classification or flux type, changing from one wire to two, a change of polarity or from DC to AC, a large change in heat input, a different joint design or backing, a new material group, and a lower preheat. The team leader checks every change against the WPS before the work goes on.

sections.title: Planning, calculations and leading the team

head: Quantity
How to work it out
Example
rows: Length of each seam × number of seams × number of passes
6 seams of 2.5 m, 2 passes each: 6 × 2.5 × 2 = 30 m
Cross-section area of weld (mm²) × length (mm) gives volume in mm³; ÷ 1 000 gives cm³; × 7.85 gives grams
Weld metal needed ÷ kg per hour
Nearly all SAW wire ends up in the weld: weld metal plus a small allowance (often 5–10%)
Wire × flux ratio (often about 1–1.5 kg per kg of wire), less what is recovered
Each quantity × its price in J$

blocks.note: Arc time is only part of the job. Set-up, dry runs, turning and repositioning, cleaning between passes, cooling to the interpass limit, tab removal and inspection often take longer than the welding. Add them before you give a time to the supervisor or the client.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Read the drawings and specification; confirm the approved WPS for each seam
Check the operators are trained (and qualified where the code asks) for SAW
Check plates, wire and flux against the WPS; set up flux storage and the flux log
Plan the order: longitudinal seams of each shell ring first, then the circumferential seams on the rolls
Work out arc time, wire and flux, and add the non-arc time to get the job time
Brief the team: set-up, roles, hold points, moving rolls, flux dust and hot slag
Inspect the first seam before the rest; check fit-up, tracking, settings, flux depth and cleaning during the work
Number each seam and record the operator, settings, wire and flux batches and inspection results
Repairs follow the repair procedure and are re-inspected before the tanks are released

head: Role
Duties
rows: Starts and stops the run, watches the meters and the bead, corrects the head position
Keeps the hopper filled with dry flux, keeps the flux layer at the right depth, runs the recovery
Watches the wire stays on the joint line; calls out readings
Writes the seam number, settings, batches, times and any problems on the record sheet

ul: Seam number on a weld map of the tank or girder.
WPS number; operator; date.
Wire and flux type and **batch numbers**, so any problem with a batch can be traced to every seam it went into.
Current, voltage and travel speed actually used; preheat and interpass readings.
Inspection and NDT results, repairs and re-inspections.

blocks.note: If your centre has no SAW machine, practise everything except striking the arc: lay a track, align a travel carriage or cutting tractor, dry-run it, time its speed over a marked length, set a stick-out and flux depth, and fill in the record. The planning, calculations and flux control are the same.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and work on it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain how SAW works and compare it with MMAW, GMAW and FCAW.
I can say which jobs suit SAW and which do not, and why it is used flat and for horizontal fillets.
I can name the hazards of SAW, including flash-through, flux dust, hot slag and moving rolls, and their controls.
I can name and check the parts of a SAW set, including the hopper, recovery system, tractor, column and boom, turning rolls and rotating earth.
I can explain DCEP, DCEN and AC in SAW and arc blow.
I can read a wire-flux classification such as F7A2-EM12K.
I can explain fused and bonded, active and neutral, acid and basic fluxes.
I can store, re-dry, recover, sieve and record flux.
I can prepare a joint for SAW, choose a backing, and fit run-on and run-off tabs.
I can set up a seam: tracking, dry run, stick-out, flux depth and settings.
I can say what current, voltage, travel speed, stick-out and wire size do to the bead.
I can work out heat input and check it against the WPS.
I can set up a circumferential seam on turning rolls, with the right offset and travel speed.
I can name SAW defects and their causes and cures, and choose the inspection and tests.
I can work out arc time, weld metal, wire, flux and cost, and plan and record a SAW job.

terms: A flux that adds manganese and silicon to the weld, more as the voltage rises
Flux made by bonding fine powders into grains; picks up moisture easily
Magnetic forces pushing the arc off line, worst at high DC currents
The time the arc is actually burning: weld length ÷ travel speed
A post and arm that hold and move the welding head over large work
The copper part that passes the welding current into the wire
A grooved copper bar clamped under a joint to hold up and shape the root
Very fine dust in flux, which must be kept out of recycled flux
Arc light breaking through a thin flux layer
The granular material that covers the arc, forms slag and protects the weld
Flux melted, cooled to a glass and crushed; picks up little moisture
Energy per mm of weld: V × A × 60 ÷ (speed × 1 000), in kJ/mm
The container on the head that holds flux and feeds it to the joint
A flux that changes the weld chemistry very little
A work connection that keeps contact while the work turns
Pieces fitted at the ends of a seam so the start and the crater are made off the job
A device that keeps the wire on the joint line
The length of wire between the end of the contact tip and the arc
Two wires, one behind the other, feeding the same pool from separate power sources
The highest point of a turning cylinder
A self-driven carriage that carries a SAW head along a seam
Powered rollers that turn a cylinder under a fixed head
One run from each side of a square-edged butt joint, each penetrating past the middle

c1.title: Water tanks for a hotel in Runaway Bay
c1.text: A shop in Runaway Bay, St Ann, is building four steel water tanks for a hotel. Each shell is 3.0 m in diameter. The circumferential seams are welded on the outside with a SAW head on a column and boom, while the shell turns on powered turning rolls. The WPS gives a travel speed of 600 mm/min. During the dry run, the shell slowly creeps along the rolls towards one end. The work lead has been fixed to the shell with an ordinary G-clamp.

c2.title: Wire and flux for fuel-tank floors in Rockfort
c2.text: Shelly-Ann looks after the SAW wire and flux at a yard in Rockfort, Kingston, for a contract to weld 25 mm plate for fuel-tank floors with multi-pass butt welds. The WPS gives the wire-flux class F7A2-EM12K, names an active, bonded flux, and asks for opened flux to be kept in a heated hopper. A new operator has been raising the arc voltage well above the WPS range on the multi-pass joints 'to get a flatter bead'. The client wants every seam to be traceable.

c3.title: Girder flange splices in Annotto Bay
c3.text: At a shop in Annotto Bay, St Mary, 12 mm flange plates for bridge girders are spliced end to end with SAW from one side, on a grooved copper backing bar clamped under the joint. On one splice the bar sagged away from the plate in the middle, and a large lump of weld metal now hangs below the joint there. A crack found in another splice shows copper-coloured streaks. For the 25 mm flanges on the next contract, the drawing shows a double-V preparation with a 6 mm root face.

c4.title: A trial plate for a barge deck in Port Antonio
c4.text: A shop in Port Antonio, Portland, is qualifying a SAW procedure for 16 mm deck plate on a barge. The draft WPS gives 4.0 mm wire, DC electrode positive, 30 V, 550 A, 400 mm/min, and a maximum heat input of 2.5 kJ/mm, because the steel must stay tough. The operator wants to slow down to 350 mm/min to fill the groove in fewer passes. Separately, the supervisor wants to build up some worn steel rollers with SAW, with as much deposit and as little penetration as possible.

c5.title: Estimating fuel-tank seams in Rocky Point
c5.text: Garth, a team leader in Rocky Point, Clarendon, is estimating the SAW work on two fuel-storage tanks. One type of seam has a weld metal cross-section of about 80 mm². The arc time for the whole job works out at about 4 hours. Wire costs J$900 per kg and flux J$700 per kg; the flux used is about 1.2 kg for each kg of wire, and he expects to use about 30 kg of wire.

questions.q: To give the WPS travel speed of 600 mm/min, about how long should one full turn of a shell take?
o: About 5 minutes
About 7.9 minutes
About 15.7 minutes
About 31.4 minutes
questions.why: The travel speed is the surface speed of the shell. Circumference = π × 3 000 = 9 425 mm; 9 425 ÷ 600 = 15.7 minutes per turn. Using the diameter alone gives 5 minutes; using the radius gives 7.9.

questions.q: What is the main risk if the creep is not put right before welding?
o: The seam moves out from under the wire and part of it is left unfused
The shell turns faster and the weld gets far too much penetration
The flux runs off the shell before the arc can reach the joint at all
The turning rolls overheat and their drive motor trips out mid-seam
questions.why: As the shell walks along the rolls, the seam moves sideways away from the fixed wire, so the arc leaves the joint line. Align the rolls or fit anti-creep rolls, then dry-run a full turn to prove the tracking.

questions.q: What should be used for the work connection instead of the G-clamp?
o: A longer lead, so that it can wind round the shell as it turns
A rotating earth that keeps sound contact as the shell turns
A second G-clamp, so there are always two contact points
A clamp on the turning-roll frame instead of on the shell
questions.why: A fixed clamp winds its cable round the turning shell or is torn off, and a clamp on the roll frame sends the current through the roll bearings. A rotating earth keeps a sound connection on the shell itself.

questions.q: What does the 2 in F7A2 tell Shelly-Ann about the weld metal?
o: It passed an impact toughness test at about −29 °C
It may be used for no more than two passes on a joint
It holds no more than about 2% manganese in total
It was tested after a two-hour stress-relief treatment
questions.why: In F7A2, 7 is the minimum tensile strength (70 000 psi), A means tested as-welded, and 2 means the weld metal met the impact test (about 27 J) at −20 °F, about −29 °C.

questions.q: Why is the operator's raised voltage a particular problem with this active flux on multi-pass joints?
o: The higher voltage drives the arc deeper and burns through the root
Active fluxes only shield the pool below about 25 V and stop above it
The extra voltage melts the wire faster than the feeder can supply it
More flux melts, so manganese and silicon build up pass by pass
questions.why: Active fluxes add manganese and silicon, and more voltage melts more flux. Over several passes these build up, making the weld harder and more crack-prone. Keep to the WPS voltage; neutral fluxes suit thick multi-pass work.

questions.q: What should be recorded for each seam so that the client can trace it?
o: The flux maker's name and the date its delivery was paid for in full
The operator, the wire and flux batch numbers, and the settings used
Only the date and whether the seam looked good when it was finished
The number of flux bags used that week across the whole of the yard
questions.why: Recording the operator, consumable batches and actual settings against each seam number means that if a batch or a setting is later found wrong, every seam it affected can be found and checked.

questions.q: Why did a lump of weld metal form below the joint where the copper bar sagged away?
o: Nothing held the pool up there, so it ran down into the gap
The copper cooled the root too fast and it shrank into a lump
The flux there was damp, so gas pushed the weld metal down
The wire wandered off the joint line onto the copper bar
questions.why: The backing bar holds up and shapes the root. Where it drops away from the plate, the deep SAW pool has nothing under it and runs through. The bar must be clamped tight along the whole seam.

questions.q: What do the copper-coloured streaks in the crack suggest?
o: The wire's copper coating is too thick and must be cleaned off first
The arc melted some of the backing bar, and copper in the weld cracks it
The flux holds copper, so it must be swapped for a basic flux at once
The plates were cut with a copper-tipped saw, leaving copper in the joint
questions.why: Copper picked up from a melted backing bar makes the weld crack as it cools. Check the settings, the bar's groove and its position so the arc never reaches the copper.

questions.q: Why does the double-V preparation for SAW have a 6 mm root face, much bigger than an MMAW preparation would?
o: A big root face holds more flux in the groove for the first run
The tracking wheel needs a wide, flat land to run along the joint
SAW penetrates so deeply that a thin root face would burn through
A thick root face means back gouging is never needed on any joint
questions.why: SAW's high current gives deep penetration, so its preparations use bigger root faces and smaller groove angles than manual processes. A thin root face would simply be burned through by the first run.

questions.q: Using heat input = V × A × 60 ÷ (speed × 1 000), what would it be at 350 mm/min, and is that allowed?
o: About 2.48 kJ/mm: within the limit, so allowed
About 2.17 kJ/mm: within the limit, so allowed
About 28.3 kJ/mm: far too high for any steel
About 2.83 kJ/mm: over the limit, not allowed
questions.why: 30 × 550 × 60 = 990 000; 350 × 1 000 = 350 000; 990 000 ÷ 350 000 = 2.83 kJ/mm, above the 2.5 kJ/mm maximum. At 400 mm/min it is 2.48. Slowing down raises heat input, so this change is not allowed.

questions.q: Which current suits building up the worn rollers, where more deposit and less penetration are wanted?
o: DC electrode positive
AC at the highest current
DC electrode negative
DC positive, short stick-out
questions.why: With DC electrode negative the wire melts faster, giving more deposit with less penetration, which suits build-up and surfacing. DC electrode positive gives the deepest penetration.

questions.q: After the trial plate passes visual inspection, why is a cross-section cut, polished and etched?
o: To measure the tensile strength of the weld across the cut face
To show the penetration, fusion and shape of each run inside
To check that the slag was fully cleaned from the cap face
To find out how much flux was used on each pass of the weld
questions.why: A macro-etch shows what cannot be seen from outside: how deep each run penetrated, whether it fused to the side walls and the run below, the bead shape (width against depth) and the heat-affected zone.

questions.q: Steel weighs about 7.85 g per cm³. About how much weld metal is in 10 m of the 80 mm² seam?
o: About 0.63 kg
About 6.3 kg
About 63 kg
About 0.8 kg
questions.why: 80 mm² × 10 000 mm = 800 000 mm³ = 800 cm³; 800 × 7.85 = 6 280 g, about 6.3 kg. Leaving out the density gives 0.8; slipping a place in the units gives 0.63 or 63.

questions.q: What is the cost of the wire and flux for the job?
questions.why: Wire: 30 kg × J$900 = J$27 000. Flux: 30 × 1.2 = 36 kg × J$700 = J$25 200. Total J$52 200. Forgetting the 1.2 ratio gives J$48 000; pricing the flux at the wire price gives J$59 400.

questions.q: How should Garth turn the 4 hours of arc time into a time for the job?
o: Use 4 hours, as the machine does the welding automatically
Halve it, as two operators can share each seam on one head
Add time for set-up, dry runs, cleaning between passes and checks
Double it, to allow for the time the flux takes to cool and set hard
questions.why: Arc time is only part of the job. Set-up, dry runs, turning, cleaning between passes, cooling to the interpass limit, tab removal and inspection often take longer than the welding itself.

questions.q: With the same current, a 3.2 mm wire is used in place of a 4.0 mm wire. What mainly happens?
o: A wider, flatter bead that bridges a poor fit-up more easily
Deeper penetration and faster melting, as the current is concentrated
Less penetration, because a thinner wire carries less heat to the joint
No change at all, since only the welding current sets the penetration
questions.why: The same current in a thinner wire is more concentrated, so it melts faster and digs deeper. A thicker wire gives a wider bead that bridges gaps better but penetrates less.

questions.q: During a circumferential run, flux spills onto a turning roll and a helper reaches across the shell to brush it off. What should the operator do?
o: Let him carry on, as long as he wears leather gauntlet gloves
Speed up the rolls so that the spill is thrown clear quickly
Tell him to use a longer brush so his hand stays further away
Stop him at once; clear spills only with the rolls stopped
questions.why: Turning rolls and a moving shell can trap and crush a hand or arm, and they do not stop for a sleeve or a glove. Use the stop button, then clear the spill with the rolls stopped.

questions.q: A 12 mm plate with square edges is welded with one SAW run from each side. What must the second run do?
o: Penetrate past the middle so that it fuses into the first run
Stay shallow so that it does not disturb the first run at all
Use a lower current than the first run, as it is only a cap run
Run on a copper bar so that the first run is not remelted at all
questions.why: In the two-run technique each run penetrates past the middle of the plate, so the runs overlap and no unfused metal is left in the centre. The WPS gives the settings that make this happen.

questions.q: Why might an engineer ask for a basic flux, rather than an acid flux, for a tank that will work at low temperatures?
o: It gives the smoothest bead at the highest travel speeds
It never picks up moisture, so it needs no oven or hopper
It gives tougher weld metal, but it must be kept very dry
It costs less and can be used straight from an open bag
questions.why: Basic fluxes give cleaner, tougher weld metal, which matters where a structure must resist brittle fracture in the cold. The price is that they are more sensitive to moisture and must be kept dry.

questions.q: Why must run-on and run-off tabs be the same steel and thickness as the job, with the same preparation?
o: So that they can be sold back as scrap together with the job's offcuts
So the arc acts as on the job and start and end faults stay on them
So the inspector can stamp the operator's number on each tab after welding
So the finished job can be lifted by the tabs after welding
questions.why: The tabs must give the arc the same conditions as the joint, so that by the time it reaches the job it is settled, and the crater at the end is left on the tab, which is cut off afterwards.
